text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's German newspapers:

- First talks between coalition and SPD over tax reform proposals without any concrete results. Talks will continue in smaller working groups. SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine says atmosphere was constructive. Coalition hopes for deal before Easter.
- Berlin man who shot and killed police officer near Hamburg apparently a member of right-wing extremist group.
- Munich Mayor Ude says opponents of controversial German Army exhibit have been organised nationally.

- Chancellery Minister Bohl says subsidies for coal industry should be reduced. Says there is no way that subsidies should exceed three billion marks by year 2000. Subsidies now amount to 10 billion marks each year and FDP wants to cut them to 2 billion.
- Cartel Office says Lufthansa prices for Frankfurt-Berlin flights are excessive.

- Tax talks will be continued with smaller working groups. Companies could see tax breaks already in 1998. Coalition and SPD move closer on some points. Tax reform aimed primarily at strengthening the economy in 1998 and only secondarily at lower top income taxes.
- Weak start in 1997 for truck manufacturers in Germany. Production for trucks over 6 tonnes falls 15 percent in January compared to year earlier.
- Ifo institute sees construction industry in protracted structural crisis.

- First top level talks between coalition and SPD begin. Goal is to have agreement for tax reform by Easter. Talks to continue on Friday. Kohl says he wants serious talks. SPD leader Lafontaine says goal is to lower supplemental wage costs.
- Transport Minister Wissmann wants to spent 450 million marks on additional bike paths in Germany, raising by 2,650 km to a total of 16,000 bike trails in Germany.
- No narrowing of gap in tax reform talks.
- Divided echo on OeTV union leader Mai's suggestion to accept reduced hours with reduced pay for public sector workers.
